analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil companies' windfall profits when crude prices spike and rebates the money to taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on March 17, 2026 with 27 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it sat without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a 50% excise tax on crude oil sold by large oil companies — those handling more than 300,000 barrels a day — whenever oil prices rise above their 2025 average level. The money collected would go into a fund and be paid out as quarterly gasoline price rebates to individual taxpayers, phasing out for higher incomes. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and has received no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, individual taxpayers would receive quarterly rebate checks funded by the new oil tax, with the largest rebates going to lower- and middle-income households; joint filers would get 150% of the individual amount. Households earning above $75,000 (or $150,000 joint) would see the rebate phase out.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Middle- and lower-income households at the pump

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise tax on each barrel of crude oil extracted or imported by large oil companies — those averaging over 300,000 barrels per day — for every dollar the price of Brent crude exceeds its 2025 average, with the threshold adjusting for inflation.

Directs the tax revenue into a 'Protect Consumers from Gas Hikes Fund' and pays it out as quarterly, fully refundable gasoline price rebates to individuals, with larger rebates (150%) for joint filers.

Phases the rebate out for higher incomes, beginning above $75,000 for single filers, $112,500 for heads of household, and $150,000 for joint filers, so the money concentrates on middle- and lower-income households.

analysis.who_pays: Large oil companies extracting or importing more than 300,000 barrels of crude per day would pay the tax whenever Brent crude trades above its 2025 average price; some of that cost could be passed to consumers at the pump.

drawbacks.text: A per-barrel tax on oil companies may be partly passed on to consumers at the pump, which could raise gasoline prices in the very quarters the bill is trying to cushion.

The tax is triggered only when Brent crude exceeds its 2025 average price, inflation-adjusted, so it would collect nothing in a year of flat or falling oil prices — leaving the rebate mechanism empty.
Rebate amounts depend on tax collections, so household payments would be unpredictable quarter to quarter and could be zero if the tax triggers no liability.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is meaningful: when oil prices spike, the companies profiting most would pay, and the money would go straight back to households to offset gasoline costs, phased out for higher incomes. The drawbacks are real: oil companies could pass part of the tax to consumers at the pump, and the base price for triggering the tax is fixed in law even though it adjusts for inflation — so in a low-price year the tax collects nothing and the rebates would be zero. The bill also never advanced to a hearing or vote, so its design was never tested or amended in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, so it died there without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on March 17, 2026 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
No further action was taken after the committee referral — no hearing, markup, or floor vote appears in the action history.
The bill attracted 27 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil companies are better off: the windfall tax was never enacted, and households never received the rebate.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on March 17, 2026 and took no further action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the action history.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, leaving it without a path to a floor vote in a chamber where the majority controls the calendar.

sides.party_line_note: All 27 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill sat in committee in a Republican-held House.

industries.note: Companies producing or importing over 300,000 barrels per day would owe a 50% excise tax on the portion of oil revenue above the 2025 Brent price baseline. This targets the windfall gains they capture when prices spike, though smaller producers fall below the threshold and pay nothing.

industries.industry: Oil refiners, marketers, and gasoline retailers
industries.note: The tax applies at the crude extraction/import stage, but to the extent oil companies pass the per-barrel tax into wholesale prices, refiners and retailers could face margin pressure or pass higher pump prices to consumers.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no hearing or markup in the Ways and Means Committee, and a House majority that controls the floor calendar, the bill is very unlikely to advance in this Congress. Its most plausible fate is to expire at the end of the session without action, though the windfall-profits-tax idea could be reintroduced in a future Congress.
